brief.title: The dip that might be a planet
brief.centralQuestion: How can a dip in starlight reveal a planet we cannot directly see?
brief.audience: Curious viewers without an astronomy background
brief.oneSentenceAnswer: A possible transit links missing light to an orbiting object's size and timing, but similar signals need to be ruled out.
brief.hook: This tiny dip could be a planet.
brief.payoff: The dip is a clue to a hidden world. The evidence has to show what made it.
brief.scope: Explain transit inference with a generic schematic and one explicitly invented numerical example.
exclusions: No new discovery or named-planet measurement is claimed in the narration.
No inference about mass, atmosphere, habitability or life.
No invented telescope dataset or observatory image.

sources.title: Detection of Planetary Transits Across a Sun-like Star
sources.institution: Author manuscript archived by arXiv; published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters
sources.version: arXiv v1, accepted manuscript; journal reference ApJ 529 (2000) L45
sources.primaryReason: The observers report their own photometric detection of two transits of HD 209458.
sources.evidenceNote: Read the abstract: transit timing agrees with prior radial-velocity observations; the light-curve shape includes limb darkening. The reel does not reuse this system's measurements.

sources.title: On the Unique Solution of Planet and Star Parameters from an Extrasolar Planet Transit Light Curve
sources.institution: Institute for Advanced Study and Princeton / Pontificia Universidad Catolica de Chile; arXiv
sources.version: arXiv v1 (2002-06-13); later journal reference ApJ 585 (2003) 1038-1055
sources.primaryReason: The authors derive the transit-geometry equations and state their assumptions.
sources.evidenceNote: Read sections 2 and 3.1-3.2.1 of v1: consecutive transits determine period; equation (1) gives depth as squared radius ratio and equation (6) its inverse.

sources.title: The Kepler Certified False Positive Table
authors: Stephen T. Bryson and the Kepler False Positive Working Group
sources.institution: NASA Ames Research Center / Kepler Science Office; MAST archive
sources.primaryReason: The mission's own working group documents its vetting process and false-positive classes.
sources.evidenceNote: Read section 1.1, printed pages 6-7: repeated transit-like events are clues; diluted background eclipsing binaries can mimic planetary transits.

claims.statement: A repeating transit-like dip can indicate a planet but does not establish one by itself.

support.supports: Transit-like signals require vetting against alternative explanations.

claims.uncertainty: A candidate interpretation, not a confirmation.
limitations: No real candidate is being analyzed in this example.

claims.statement: An appropriately aligned planet crossing its star can cause a measured dip in starlight.

support.supports: An observed example of this mechanism; the animation generalizes it.

claims.uncertainty: The illustration explains the mechanism rather than reproducing those observations.
limitations: A crossing must occur along the observer's line of sight; most orbit orientations do not transit.

claims.statement: Consecutive transits of the same planet reveal its orbital period.

support.supports: Consecutive events identify the period used by the model.

claims.uncertainty: Assumes the events belong to one planet and no intervening transit was missed.
limitations: Gaps or other periodic sources can confuse the interpretation.

claims.statement: In an idealized uniform-star model, 1% blocked light corresponds to a planet-to-star radius ratio of 0.1.

support.supports: Depth equals squared radius ratio in the specified idealization.

claims.uncertainty: Exact within these assumptions; illustrative input, not an observed measurement.
limitations: Real fits account for limb darkening, grazing geometry and extra light.

calculation.result: Rp = 0.1 Rstar, or 10% of the stellar radius; no absolute radius is inferred.
assumptions: Uniform projected stellar brightness (no limb darkening)
Opaque dark planet fully within the stellar disk at mid-transit
No blended light or measurement noise

claims.statement: A background eclipsing binary diluted by brighter target-star light can mimic a planetary transit.

support.locator: Section 1.1, Background Eclipsing or Transiting Object, printed page 7
support.supports: The mission documents this astrophysical false-positive mechanism.

claims.uncertainty: One possible alternative; the source describes several others.
limitations: This is a conceptual example of a contaminant, not a verdict on a particular target.

beats.narration: This tiny dip could be a planet.

shot.direction: Open on a clean brightness-versus-time trace with one shallow dip. Highlight the dip without revealing a planet yet. Label both axes; do not present fabricated telescope points.
visualCaveats: Stylized trace; dip depth and timescale are not measurements.
shot.continuity: Retain this trace below the geometry in the next beat.

beats.narration: A telescope records starlight. If a planet crosses the star from our viewpoint, the measured brightness falls.

shot.direction: Show a dark disk moving across a uniform stellar disk from the observer's view. Advance a cursor along the retained light curve; dimming begins at first overlap and ends after the disk exits.
visualCaveats: Resolved disks illustrate geometry; the telescope measurement can be unresolved.
Do not show light physically dimming everywhere in space.
shot.continuity: Use the same star and disk in all single-planet shots.

beats.narration: Matching dips at regular intervals can reveal its orbital period, if each orbit's transit is observed.

shot.direction: Extend the trace to show three equally spaced dips. Put a bracket between consecutive mid-transit times labeled one orbit. Show a small orbital inset with observer direction; compress elapsed time visibly.
visualCaveats: Assume no missed transits and the same object in each crossing.
Animation seconds do not represent the orbital period.
shot.continuity: Keep the same trace's baseline; use matching midpoints for the interval brackets.

beats.narration: Depth carries another clue. In this simplified model, a one-percent dip means the planet's radius is one tenth of the star's.

shot.direction: Freeze full overlap against a uniformly bright star. Draw labeled radius segments with a 10-to-1 length ratio. Plot 100% and 99% flux ticks beside the dip; mark the cropped vertical axis. Hold the result long enough to read with its assumptions.
onScreenText: Uniform star; full overlap; no extra light
visualCaveats: Use radius ratio, not mass or area ratio, for the 10% label.
The 1% value is invented for arithmetic clarity; never label it HD 209458 data.
The stellar disk is uniform only for this idealization.
shot.continuity: Retain the same star center; adjust the planet radius to precisely 0.1 of stellar radius for this labeled example.

beats.narration: The dip tells us light is missing. But what blocked it?

shot.direction: Cut to Rowan in his bookshelf study for this single question. Return to the diagram as Titan answers.
visualCaveats: The interview poses the question; the following model illustrates the alternative.
shot.continuity: Leave the light curve on the same dip for the return cut.

beats.narration: A faint pair of eclipsing stars can mimic that signal. Astronomers check for these lookalikes.

shot.direction: Split the model into target star plus a fainter background stellar pair. One star eclipses the other. Combine their light into one schematic aperture and show a shallow dip. Keep the target star visible so dilution is understandable.
visualCaveats: Separate the conceptual components for explanation; do not imply the telescope resolves the blended pair.
This is one alternative, not a complete vetting procedure.
shot.continuity: Use a clear cut to prevent the planet model from silently becoming the binary model.

beats.narration: The dip is a clue to a hidden world. The evidence has to show what made it.

shot.direction: Return to the original trace beside the two explicitly labeled explanations. Finish on the dip with a candidate label. Do not stamp either model confirmed or add a discovery claim.
visualCaveats: No real candidate has been confirmed by this worked example.
shot.continuity: Match the opening trace and settle on the same dip.
